newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - South Africa's wage costs - By E.Osborn.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - South Africa's wage costs - By E.Osborn.

text.p: By Edward Osborn, consultant to Edey, Rogers (Pty) Ltd

The fairly innocuous throw-away remarks by the Reserve Bank in its latest Quarterly Bulletin about wage costs and employment have thrown the media into a frenzy of editorial moralising and excited outraged calls for central bank control by labour.

The two relevant points made were the comment -- almost a truism -- that to the extent that the Basic Conditions of Employment Bill add to the costs of labour there could be adverse employment implications (note "could" instead of "will'), and, secondly, the coincidence of a rise in employment with a slowdown in the rate of growth of nominal unit labour costs.

The latter coincidence is wilfully construed as causal and there is, indeed, such a hint in the Bank's review. It is therefore supportive of the argument against any statutory induced increment to unit labour costs. The Bank's orthodox position has always been clear, namely that increases in labour costs should be matched by improvements in productivity, thereby keeping unit labour costs constant, competitiveness intact and inflation subdued.

Unfortunately the facts, as reported by the Central Statistical Service, do not support the Bank's statement that there was an increase in employment in the fourth quarter. Total non-agricultural employment actually fell by 7,000 in the last quarter although there was an overall increase in manufacturing of 5,000. This was confined to the food and textile sectors. On the other hand there was an overall net fall of 5,000 in the second half of the year in manufacturing.

The actual evidence of causality is therefore marginal and unconvincing although, no doubt, it is valid in theory to a degree. And yet the longer term trends in employment -- for example, a drop of over 100,000 in manufacturing since 1990 -- have been profoundly disappointing because of their social consequences in terms of deprivation, poverty and crime. We have to look to larger structural forces at work and move away from this myopic preoccupation with unit labour costs and labour inflexibility as the source of our economic ills.

Structural change is manifest in the manufacturing sector, as revealed in the published indices of manufacturing output. It is essentially that of the trend towards capital intensity in manufacturing and the stagnation of domestic industries exposed to external competition. Oddly enough the authors of the Gear (Growth, Employment and Redistribution) document were unaware of this, for otherwise they would not have made the wildly optimistic projections of employment opportunity created by industrial development that they did.

The 28 sub-sectors of manufacturing output, as published by the CSS, have been grouped into nine bundles of associated industries for the purposes of manageable analysis. Such groupings show that the overall growth of manufacturing output of only 5.5 percent by the first quarter of 1997 since the base period of 1990 is due to the highly capital-intensive chemicals and basic metals industries. With the temporary exception of wood and furniture, possibly associated with the diaspora of offices from the Johannesburg CBD, all other industrial groupings are at levels below or, at best, about the production level of 1990, six years ago.

A dominant factor in the chemicals industry has been the rise of the petroleum refining industry which, due to the considerable addition of refining capacity in recent years, is currently at an index of about 150, i.e. a growth of 50 percent since 1990. In the case of basic metals, the non-ferrous plants have an index of 180, or 80 percent above the 1990 level.

The factors that have been at play are basically the exposure to international competition through tariff liberalisation, dumping and illegal imports and the trends towards capital-intensive development of the chemicals industries and the major basic metals industries. These latter industries are either naturally capable of standing up to international competition because of the technologies involved or are the logical extensions of the metals beneficiary process with markets abroad. Their establishment has been assisted by such now-expired export incentive devices as Section 37 E of the Income Tax Act with its accelerated depreciation allowances and the GEIS - the General Export Incentive Scheme.

The structural trends are most likely to continue and not be reversed. The implication is that manufacturing growth is likely to continue arising from the not insubstantial programme of investment in capital-intensive plants that have already been publicised but, in the process, there is unlikely to be an accompanying proportionate rise in employment. But, furthermore, the spread of manufacturing industry that has already shown itself to be sensitive to foreign competition will have to go through more cost cutting and rationalisation programmes in order to be competitive and to survive. However, industries, like furniture manufacture and some of the food manufacturing industry will continue to enjoy natural locational advantages and be able to cope. The net overall addition to manufacturing employment in this whole process may well be negligible.

In the last four years, since the start of the economic recovery, manufacturing production as a whole has grown by 14.4 percent, but employment in manufacturing has fallen by six percent. This is the very reverse of what is assumed to be the situation in government's Gear macroeconomic strategy. Given the trends as identified above there is a fair possibility that the experience of the last four years can be repeated in the next three. So, instead of the additional 227,000 jobs expected in Gear, there could be an effective loss of some 150,000 jobs. The economic consequences of this are serious in terms of a deflationary multiplier impact on the domestic economy. However, government will, no doubt, have to introduce various fire-fighting measures along the way, like the recent intention to impose footwear import quotas on non-members of the World Trade Organisation, in which case employment in manufacturing might be held at its present level in 1997 and then the overall loss on the base period used in the

It is a further open question as to whether the rationalisation forced on exposed domestic firms has been due to high wage costs, or as much to the composite productivity, or lack thereof, of management, high capital costs, labour costs and input cost -- much of which should be taken care of through a depreciated rand.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
